name: Jang Mo Jip
body: The seolleongtang, ox bone soup, remains a longtime favorite at Jangmo Jip. Orange County food writers have written about it for years. But Jangmo Jip’s other soups, such as the soothing samgyetang, or ginseng chicken soup with purple rice, and the beef brisket, are worthwhile. Most people order soup, but other popular items include the tender mandu and pork belly bossam wrapped in lettuce seasoned with ssamjang.

name: The Source
body: A Gen Z epicenter for Korean culture and K-pop, The Source in Buena Park grew into the place where fans pick up coveted albums, collectibles and Korean street food. Notable spots include Myungrang Hot Dog, Old Ferry Donut from Seoul with its custard-filled creme brulee and pistachio doughnuts, and even more things to eat tucked into two food courts. Boba shops like Ding Tea embrace the K-pop frenzy with special events featuring BTS and other bands printed on paper cup sleeves. The limited quantities make sleeves collectibles, with people lining up for hours just for a single cup.

name: Jinsol Gukbap
body: This is the place to slurp on Busan-style pork bone broth simmered for 24 hours. The boiling hot milky white soup is dotted with chunks of tender pork meat and served with banchan like cabbage kimchi, raw onions, jalapenos, chili sauce, and seasoned chives. Purple-tinged rice and noodles arrive on the side for the soup. Another Jinsol opened in Stanton recently and the chain boasts two locations in LA’s Koreatown as well.

name: Han Yang
body: This restaurant looks like a converted car hop. But instead of serving burgers and other American food, Han Yang dishes out bowls of beef, ox bone, ground pork mandu (dumpling), and galbitang. The bibim naengmyeon — cold buckwheat noodle dish with a sweet and spicy house sauce comes garnished with lettuce, cucumber, roasted sesame and boiled egg, while the kong guksu — iced soybean sauce noodles with cucumber and tomato, is another cold noodle dish worth trying. Vegetarian dishes include the rice hot plate with seasoned thistle, egg yolk, and kkakdugi, or pickled radish. A gondeure sauce gets mixed in to meld all the flavors. Also written as “gondre,” the Korean thistle originated as a wild mountain herb but is now widely grown in greenhouses in Korea.

name: Hsiang Yuen Chinese Restaurant
body: Though technically just outside of Orange County in Artesia, Hsiang Yuen Restaurant is worth the stop. The small mom-and-pop restaurant opened in 1983. It’s known for its jajangmyeon, a pork-based black bean sauce dotted with chopped onions and bits of green zucchini. The noodles are springy, sopping up the dark sauce. The crispy fried sesame balls with sweet black beans are a poppable dessert. Though be warned they’re scorchingly hot when they first emerge from the fryer.

name: Mo Ran Gak Restaurant
body: For 24 years, Mo Ran Gak has remained a staple in Garden Grove for Korean barbecue and is still one of the few places to find North Korean-style noodles called mul naengmyeon. The cold buckwheat noodles are a specialty of the restaurant, along with the spicy bibim naengmyeon with crunchy bites of radish, cucumber, and Asian pear. They’re best served with grilled galbi, marinated beef short ribs.

name: Gaenali Bon Ga
body: The bossam jungsik is what most first time diners order since the tender pork belly wrapped in lettuce is approachable and easily customizable, but more adventurous diners opt for the octopus bibimbap and the spicy raw marinated crab, yangnyeom gejang. Gaenali Bon Ga also serves Korean comfort food such as budae jjigae, or army stew, a spicy pot filled with ramen, kimchi, hot dogs, and tofu. Also try the monkfish soup and claypot galbitang.

name: Peking Gourmet
body: Since it opened in 1985, Peking Gourmet is one of the oldest Korean Chinese food restaurants in Orange County. The interior resembles a typical Chinese American restaurant circa the 90s and the menu offers the typical broccoli beef, egg rolls, wonton soup, and chicken fried rice. But the best representation of the Korean Chinese fusion is found in the jajangmyeon. The fermented black bean sauce noodles served with tender bites of pork originated in Incheon, Korea, by Chinese immigrants.

name: Yigah
body: Yigah already made its mark on the 38 Essential Orange County Restaurants for its expansive Korean comfort food menu. Soups include the seolleongtang made with simmered ox bones, the green onion-laden braised beef ribs, and gamjatang, a spicy pork back-bone stew flavored with perilla leaves and huge potato chunks. Most diners order a couple of dishes like the crispy katsu cutlet or octopus bibimbap for the table to share, along with bubbling bowls of soup.

name: Sookdal
body: Since opening in 2014, the Korean barbecue export now boasts more than 40 locations in South Korea, Japan, Southeast Asia, and the U.S. In Orange County, the Garden Grove location remains the busiest. Sookdal means “experienced master” and echoes the restaurant’s attention to using aged meat. The beef brisket, bavette, and ribeye are all dry-aged. The pork set with pork neck, pork belly, and marinated pork ribs features wet-aged meat. The sides include Korean shabu-shabu, grilled cheese, sliced pineapple, and mushrooms to grill at the table.

name: Furai Chicken
body: Furai Chicken grew so popular that the Korean fried chicken stall upgraded from its food court space at Zion Market to a standalone space on Yale Avenue in Irvine. The crispy original fried chicken and soy garlic-coated wings are served with pickled daikon and jalapenos. As for the sides, stick with the potato wedges. The dining room is sparse, which means tends to do more of takeout orders.

name: Jopok Topokki
body:
Located inside the food court at the most well-stocked H Mart in Irvine, this Jopok Topokki is much smaller than its sister restaurant on Commonwealth in Buena Park. At both locations, the rapokki, a combination of rice cakes and ramen in kimchi broth and fish cakes, remains the most popular item, even for takeout orders. Since it’s in a grocery store, the crisp waffle-like dessert taiyaki comes stuffed with nutella, custard, or red bean, making for a scrumptious pre- or post-shopping snack.

name: Moo Bong Ri
body:
The popular K-town soondae outpost expanded to OC with a location inside H Mart in Irvine. Its grew locally, which led to another expansion to Irvine Plaza on Barranca Parkway. The beef short rib soup and the beef back rib soup with glass noodles are the more approachable bowls for first timers but diners-in-the-know come for the soondae, Korean pork blood sausage. It’s served sliced or simmered in soup, which can also be ordered spicy. The soondae sampler is another option to share with the table.

name: Dosirak Express
body: This is the ideal fast-casual stop for Korean homestyle stews, lunches, and rice bowls. Dosirak is the Korean version of a lunchtime bento box. The shop’s large refrigerator case is stocked with seaweed soup, pickled vegetables, and cold noodle salads to take away. For other dishes, orders can be placed at the counter or online. The dosirak and rice bowls with glazed salmon or bulgogi are the most popular. Another popular item is the gimbap, which can be rolled with tuna, spicy pork, bulgogi, shrimp, or vegetables.

name: Hanshin Pocha
body: Inspired by Korean food wagons that evolved into outdoor food stalls, Hanshin Pocha serves street food and savory bar bites that pair well with soju and beer. Wedged in a cluster of casual restaurants near an Albertsons at Quail Hill Shopping Center, the location seems like an unusual place to set up a pocha. But people (many of whom are UCI students) wait in groups outside for tables. The tteokbokki (spicy rice cakes) and kimchi jeongol (kimchi hot pot), along with the pub-friendly whole fried chicken and stir-fried spicy squid are easily shareable. Dishes can also be taken to-go.
